 Bhai Dooj 2026 timing: Check most auspicious time for tilak today; know exact puja timings and duration (image: canva) Bhai Dooj 2026 will be observed on Wednesday, November 11.
 Tilak muhurat in New Delhi is from 1:10 pm to 3:20 pm.
 The festival celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.

 Bhai Dooj, one of the most cherished festivals celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters, will be observed on Wednesday, November 11, 2026. Also known as Bhaiya Dooj, Bhau Beej and Yama Dwitiya, the festival falls on the second day of the Shukla Paksha in the Hindu month of Kartika.  The most important ritual of the day is the tilak ceremony, during which sisters apply a ceremonial mark on their brothers' foreheads and pray for their long life, happiness and prosperity. Brothers, in turn, express their affection by giving gifts and spending time with their sisters. 
 According to the Hindu Panchang, the auspicious Aparahna period for the Bhai Dooj tilak ceremony in New Delhi will begin at 1:10 pm and end at 3:20 pm. The ritual window will last for two hours and 10 minutes. 
 Bhai Dooj 2026: Date and auspicious tilak muhurat 
 Here are the key timings for Bhai Dooj 2026: 
 Festival: Bhai Dooj / Bhaiya Dooj 
 Date: Wednesday, November 11, 2026 
 Bhai Dooj Aparahna time: 1:10 pm to 3:20 pm 
 Duration: 2 hours and 10 minutes 
 Dwitiya Tithi begins: 2:00 pm on November 10, 2026 
 Dwitiya Tithi ends: 3:53 pm on November 11, 2026 
 Note: All timings are based on the local time of New Delhi. Panchang calculations may vary slightly across locations. 
 Bhai Dooj 2026: Significance of the tilak ceremony 
 The tilak ceremony is the central ritual of Bhai Dooj. Sisters apply a mark on their brothers' foreheads and pray for their health, safety, happiness and long life. The ritual is accompanied by prayers and Aarti, symbolising the affection and protective bond shared by siblings. 
 Traditionally, sisters prepare a puja thali with items such as roli, rice grains, sweets, a diya and other ritual essentials. After applying tilak, they perform Aarti and offer sweets to their brothers. In many families, sisters also tie a sacred thread around their brothers' wrists.  Brothers then give gifts to their sisters as a gesture of love and appreciation. The exchange of blessings and gifts makes the occasion a celebration of family ties and mutual affection. 
 Bhai Dooj puja rituals and traditions 
 On Bhai Dooj, sisters traditionally wake up early, take a bath and prepare for the day's rituals. Some observe a fast or take a religious vow before performing the puja. They invite their brothers for the ceremony and arrange the puja thali.  The tilak is applied during the auspicious Aparahna period, followed by Aarti and prayers for the brother's well-being. Sweets and a festive meal are often shared after the ceremony. 
 The customs may differ from one region and family to another, but the central tradition remains the same: sisters pray for their brothers' well-being, while brothers reaffirm their affection and support. 
 Why is Bhai Dooj also called Yama Dwitiya? 
 Bhai Dooj is closely associated with the legend of Lord Yama, the god of death, and his sister, Goddess Yamuna.  According to the traditional story, Goddess Yamuna repeatedly invited her brother Yama to visit her home. On the day he finally accepted her invitation, she welcomed him with a ceremonial tilak, performed Aarti and served him a meal. 
 Pleased by her affection and hospitality, Yama offered her a boon. Yamuna asked that brothers who visit their sisters and receive their blessings on this day be protected from the fear of untimely death and blessed with a long life.  Yama granted her wish. This is why the festival is also known as Yama Dwitiya, and why the bond between brothers and sisters is celebrated with special religious significance. 
 Religious significance of bathing in the Yamuna 
 Bathing in the Yamuna River is considered especially auspicious on Bhai Dooj. According to religious beliefs, a holy dip on this day brings blessings, spiritual merit and prosperity.  The tradition is also linked to the legend of Yama and Yamuna. Devotees believe that observing the prescribed rituals and seeking the blessings of the divine siblings can bring protection and well-being. 
 Bhai Dooj is celebrated under several names across India, including Bhaiya Dooj, Bhau Beej, Bhai Dwitiya, Bhatra Dwitiya and Bhathru Dwithiya. Despite regional differences in customs, the festival continues to honour the enduring bond between brothers and sisters.
